source_title: Sample Interview: Smallholder Logistics and the Aggregation Problem
text:
Host: Kwame Mensah is the founder of AgriLink, based in Accra. Kwame, good to have you.

Kwame Mensah: Good to be here.

Host: Give us the origin story.

Kwame Mensah: I grew up in a farming household in the Ashanti Region. My mother grew tomatoes. And the thing I understood before I understood anything about business is that she was never paid a price that had anything to do with what tomatoes sold for in Accra. There were four or five intermediaries between her and the market, and each one took a margin for solving a real problem, which was aggregation and transport. I did not think the intermediaries were villains. I thought the structure was inefficient.

Host: And AgriLink was founded when?

Kwame Mensah: 2019. I had been working in supply chain for a brewing company for five years, which is where I learned how commodity logistics actually functions. We started with forty-two farmers in one district.

Host: What does the product do?

Kwame Mensah: At the simplest level we aggregate produce from smallholder farmers and sell it to institutional buyers, hotels, processors, supermarket chains. The technology is a marketplace and a logistics layer, but I want to be careful because the technology is genuinely the easy part. What makes it work is that we guarantee a price at planting time rather than at harvest. A farmer who knows in March what she will be paid in July can make decisions. That is the entire product, and everything else is machinery to support that promise.

Host: How do you handle the risk of guaranteeing a price?

Kwame Mensah: Badly, at first. In 2021 we guaranteed prices on a maize volume we could not place, the market moved against us, and we lost about six hundred thousand dollars in one season. That nearly ended the company. What we do now is that we only guarantee volume we have a matching offtake agreement for. So we sell forward before we buy forward. It is less exciting and we grow more slowly and we are still here.

Host: How many farmers today?

Kwame Mensah: A little over thirty-one thousand across Ghana and Cote d'Ivoire, as of the end of 2024. Average income increase for a farmer in their second season with us is around thirty-four percent, and I would flag that we measure that against their own prior season rather than against a control group, so treat it as directional.

Host: You have talked publicly about resisting pressure to become a lender.

Kwame Mensah: Every investor asks. The margins on agricultural credit are visible and attractive and the data we hold makes underwriting easy. My concern is that the moment we lend to a farmer we are also the buyer of her crop, and those two relationships are in tension. If she has a bad season, am I her creditor or her partner? I have not found a structure I am comfortable with. We partner with two banks instead and we do not touch the loan book.

Host: Final thought?

Kwame Mensah: Agriculture punishes people who move fast and break things, because the thing you break is somebody's only income for a year. The cycle time is a season. You get one experiment per year, so you had better think carefully before you run it.
